intro.title: AbortController & Cleanup in useEffect
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple Angular component that fetches and displays user data from a mock API. You'll learn how to use the AbortController to cancel ongoing HTTP requests when a component is destroyed, preventing memory leaks and errors. The core concept is implementing cleanup logic within Angular's lifecycle hooks, specifically using ngOnDestroy to abort fetch operations. This involves working with TypeScript, Angular's HttpClient, and the AbortController API to manage asynchronous data fetching safely.
intro.usecase: In real-world Angular applications, the pattern of aborting requests with AbortController is critical for managing side effects in components. This is commonly used in dashboards with live-updating charts, where a user quickly changes filters or time ranges, and you must cancel the previous data fetch to avoid outdated or conflicting data. It also applies to search inputs with debounced API calls, where typing rapidly should cancel pending requests to ensure the UI displays only the latest results. Proper cleanup prevents memory leaks and race conditions, ensuring a responsive and reliable user experience in interactive features like data tables, autocomplete fields, or multi-step wizards.

objectives: Initialize an AbortController instance within an Angular component
Integrate the AbortController signal into an HTTP request using HttpClient
Configure the cleanup function in ngOnDestroy to abort pending requests
Apply the AbortController pattern to prevent memory leaks in component subscriptions
Construct a service method that automatically cancels requests when components are destroyed
Manipulate component state only when HTTP requests complete successfully
Implement error handling for aborted requests to maintain application stability

steps.title: Import required Angular modules and RxJS utilities
steps.instruction: Import HttpClientModule, HttpClient, Component, OnInit, and OnDestroy from '@angular/core', and Subject and takeUntil from 'rxjs'.
steps.hint: Use import statements at the top of your TypeScript file. Remember to import from the correct packages: '@angular/core' and 'rxjs'.

steps.expectedOutcome: The necessary imports for HTTP requests and reactive programming are added to the file.
successCriteria: HttpClientModule, HttpClient, Component, OnInit, OnDestroy are imported from '@angular/core', and Subject, takeUntil are imported from 'rxjs'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've imported some of the required items, but not all. Check that you have HttpClientModule, HttpClient, Component, OnInit, OnDestroy from '@angular/core', and Subject, takeUntil from 'rxjs'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The imports are missing or incorrect. You need to import HttpClientModule, HttpClient, Component, OnInit, OnDestroy from '@angular/core', and Subject, takeUntil from 'rxjs'.

steps.title: Create the main component class
steps.instruction: Create a component class named DataComponent that implements OnInit and OnDestroy interfaces.
steps.hint: Use the @Component decorator with an empty selector and template for now. Define the class with proper TypeScript syntax.
steps.seedCode:
import { Component, OnInit, OnDestroy } from '@angular/core';

// Create DataComponent class here
steps.expectedOutcome: A DataComponent class is created with empty ngOnInit and ngOnDestroy methods.
successCriteria: DataComponent class exists, implements OnInit and OnDestroy, and has empty ngOnInit and ngOnDestroy methods.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the class implements both OnInit and OnDestroy interfaces and has empty methods for both.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've created a class named DataComponent with @Component decorator and implements both interfaces.

steps.title: Initialize component properties and state
steps.instruction: Inside the DataComponent class, declare properties for data (any[]), loading (boolean), error (string), and a Subject for cleanup (Subject<void>).
steps.hint: Use TypeScript property declarations with appropriate types and initial values. The Subject will help manage cleanup later.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now has typed properties for data, loading state, error handling, and a cleanup Subject.
successCriteria: Properties data (any[]), loading (boolean), error (string), and destroy$ (Subject<void>) are declared with initial values.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've declared some properties, but check if all required ones (data, loading, error, destroy$) are present with correct types.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component properties aren't properly declared. Make sure to declare data, loading, error, and a Subject for cleanup with appropriate types.

steps.title: Inject HttpClient service
steps.instruction: In the DataComponent constructor, inject the HttpClient service to make it available for HTTP calls.
steps.hint: Add a constructor parameter with the HttpClient type and use Angular's dependency injection.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: injecting a service
constructor(private http: HttpClient) {}
steps.expectedOutcome: The DataComponent constructor now has HttpClient injected, enabling HTTP requests.
successCriteria: HttpClient is injected as a private parameter in the DataComponent constructor.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure HttpClient is injected as a constructor parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the constructor syntax. You need to inject HttpClient as a parameter.

steps.title: Create the fetchData method
steps.instruction: Inside the DataComponent class, create a method named fetchData that uses HttpClient.get() to fetch data from an API endpoint.
steps.hint: The method should be public and use the injected HttpClient instance to make a GET request. You can use a placeholder URL like 'https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts' for now.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now has a fetchData method that can be called to retrieve data from an API.
successCriteria: The fetchData method is defined in the DataComponent class and uses this.http.get() with a URL string.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the method is named fetchData and uses this.http.get() with a URL string.
steps.feedbackWrong: The fetchData method is missing or doesn't use HttpClient.get(). Remember to create a method that makes an HTTP GET request.

steps.title: Add RxJS pipe with takeUntil operator
steps.instruction: In your fetchData method, add a .pipe(takeUntil(this.destroy$)) to the HTTP observable chain to enable cleanup.
steps.expectedOutcome: The fetchData method now includes takeUntil(this.destroy$) in the observable pipe chain.
successCriteria: The HTTP observable chain includes .pipe(takeUntil(this.destroy$)) before .subscribe().
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure takeUntil(this.destroy$) is inside .pipe() and placed before .subscribe().
steps.feedbackWrong: The takeUntil operator wasn't added correctly. Check that it's chained with .pipe() before .subscribe().

steps.title: Handle successful data response
steps.instruction: Inside the fetchData method's subscribe callback, update the component's data property with the received response.
steps.hint: Assign the data parameter from the subscribe callback to this.data.
steps.expectedOutcome: The fetchData method will now store the HTTP response data in the component's data property for use in the template.
successCriteria: The subscribe callback assigns the data parameter to this.data
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're assigning the data parameter from the subscribe callback to this.data.
steps.feedbackWrong: The subscribe callback should update the component's data property with the received response.

steps.title: Handle error responses
steps.instruction: In the fetchData method's subscribe call, add an error callback to handle HTTP errors and update the component's error property.
steps.hint: The subscribe method can take a second callback function for errors. Inside it, set this.error to an appropriate error message.
steps.expectedOutcome: The fetchData method now includes error handling that will update an error property when the HTTP request fails.
successCriteria: The subscribe call has a second callback function for errors that sets this.error to an error message.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've added the error callback as the second parameter to subscribe and are updating this.error with an appropriate message.
steps.feedbackWrong: The error handling isn't quite right. Remember that subscribe can take two callbacks - one for success and one for errors. Add the error callback to handle failed requests.

steps.title: Implement ngOnInit lifecycle hook
steps.instruction: Inside the DataComponent class, implement the ngOnInit method to call the fetchData method when the component initializes.
steps.hint: The ngOnInit method is called automatically by Angular after the component is created. You can call this.fetchData() inside it.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ngOnInit method will be implemented to trigger data fetching when the component initializes.
successCriteria: The ngOnInit method contains a call to this.fetchData()
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started implementing ngOnInit, but make sure to call this.fetchData() inside the method.
steps.feedbackWrong: The ngOnInit method should call this.fetchData() to trigger data fetching on component initialization.

steps.title: Implement ngOnDestroy cleanup
steps.instruction: In the ngOnDestroy method, call the next() and complete() methods on the destroy$ Subject to properly clean up subscriptions.
steps.hint: Use this.destroy$.next() followed by this.destroy$.complete() inside the ngOnDestroy method.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ngOnDestroy method will properly clean up the destroy$ Subject, preventing memory leaks when the component is destroyed.
successCriteria: ngOnDestroy method contains this.destroy$.next() and this.destroy$.complete() calls.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to call both next() and complete() on the destroy$ Subject. Both are needed for proper cleanup.
steps.feedbackWrong: The ngOnDestroy method should contain cleanup logic. You need to call this.destroy$.next() to emit a value and this.destroy$.complete() to mark the Subject as completed.

steps.title: Create the component template
steps.instruction: Add the component's template with sections to display loading, error, and data states. Use the existing component properties to conditionally show each section.
steps.hint: Create a template with *ngIf directives to show different UI sections based on the component's state properties.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a complete template that displays different UI sections based on the component's state properties.
successCriteria: Template includes sections for loading, error, and data display using *ngIf directives
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.

steps.instruction: In the AppModule, add HttpClientModule to the imports array to enable HTTP functionality throughout your application.
steps.hint: Look for the @NgModule decorator in your app.module.ts file and add HttpClientModule to the imports array.
steps.expectedOutcome: The AppModule will be configured to use Angular's HTTP client, allowing your DataComponent to make HTTP requests.
successCriteria: HttpClientModule is added to the imports array in the AppModule decorator.
